(a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I. A piecewise C^1 worldline is a piecewise C^1 curve whose tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future timelike, and a C^k worldline is a worldline whose parametrization is C^k; C^2 regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of this page available. The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve s |-> x(-s), which is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to it. Current required supplier statement (batch3, homesr-worldlines-and-clocks, computed level7): Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I. A piecewise C^1 worldline is a piecewise C^1 curve whose tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future timelike, and a C^k worldline is a worldline whose parametrization is C^k; C^2 regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of this page available. The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve s |-> x(-s), which is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to it.
